\title{Does Crowd Evidence Help Flood-Aware Routing? An Offline Routing Prototype and a Replay Study on the Chennai Road Network}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Pragatish N}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{\textless Department\textgreater} \\

\begin{abstract}
Navigation apps in Indian cities now display crowd-reported waterlogging, but they do not say how much a report should change a route, how long it should count, or what to do when reports are absent. We built a routing prototype for Chennai that keeps a flood belief for every road segment, formed from a static susceptibility prior and age-decayed, source-weighted reports, routes on a pessimistic index of that belief, and attaches a decision record from which explanations are rendered and checked. We asked whether crowd reports, as opposed to the prior, improve routes. On the OpenStreetMap graph of Chennai with \NObs{} observations from the 2015 floods and \NOD{} origin--destination pairs, all routes were scored under one reference belief. The default commuter setting changed \ChgThree{} routes at a \DetThree\% mean detour. A baseline that blocks high-probability edges and adds a soft penalty exposed routes to less risk than our method at the same risk weight. Against held-out official reports, crowd evidence moved routes toward reported edges, and it made the belief's Brier score worse than the prior alone. We also show that our first pessimistic index lowered caution after a single weak report, and replace it with a Beta posterior quantile that cannot. Finally, we assemble a prototype dataset of time-stamped street-level flood evidence with negatives from fragmented public sources, and show why it cannot yet test rain-driven closures. The results describe one historical event; they do not establish benefit or safety in live use.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Calibration, crowdsourcing, flood hazards, mobile computing, route planning, uncertainty.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Pluvial floods cut urban road networks in ways that travel-time routing does not see. Hydrodynamic and network studies show disconnection of intra-urban roads~\cite{yin2016shanghai,zhou2022connectivity}, abrupt network-wide failure from local flooding~\cite{wang2019percolation}, and longer emergency response times~\cite{green2017emergency,coles2017york}; depth--disruption functions relate water depth to safe speed~\cite{pregnolato2017depth}. Chennai flooded severely in 2015 and again in 2023~\cite{vanoldenborgh2016chennai,radhakrishnan2024chennai}, and its built-up area keeps growing~\cite{devi2019sprawl}.

Consumer navigation has started to respond. Google reported that India produced more flood-related alerts on Maps in 2025 than any other country~\cite{ramani2025maps}, and Mappls offers waterlogging and flood-alert report categories~\cite{mappls2026post}. In Chennai, a crowd flood map ran as a pilot from 2017 to 2019~\cite{urbanrisklab2019riskmap}, and a volunteer street-marking effort recorded more than 2,500 flooded streets within a day in 2015~\cite{naik2016flooded}. What these services do not document is how a report should change a route: how much weight a single report deserves, how quickly it should fade, how sparse evidence should be treated, and how the choice should be explained. Crowd reports are also known to be sparse, uneven across neighbourhoods and of varying accuracy~\cite{senaratne2017vgi,esparza2023imbalance,liu2023wazecoverage}.

We built a prototype that makes these choices explicit and then tested whether they matter. It fuses a susceptibility prior with decaying reports, routes on a pessimistic index whose strength is set per user class, separates slowdown from harm in the edge cost, and returns a decision record that explanation layers must respect. We ask three questions. RQ1: does the belief-aware cost change routes on a real city graph, and at what travel-time cost? RQ2: do crowd reports add anything to routing or to the belief beyond the static prior? RQ3: does the pessimistic index behave as intended when evidence is sparse?

The contribution is a systems integration and an application case study, not a new algorithm. Every component has precedent, which Section~\ref{sec:related} credits. Specifically, the paper offers:
\begin{itemize}
\item An open design that combines a decaying, source-weighted flood belief, a class-specific pessimistic index, a cost that separates slowdown from harm, and a decision record with a symbolic gate on generated explanations (Sections~\ref{sec:model}--\ref{sec:system}).
\item Three analytical observations: a time-proportional penalty caps an edge's cost at $1+\lambda s$ times free-flow time; a Wald-type pessimistic index decreases after one report from a source whose reliability is below about 0.63; and a Beta posterior quantile, which replaced it, never decreases after a positive report (Propositions~\ref{prop:cap} and~\ref{prop:mono}, Observation~\ref{obs:dip}).
\item A replay evaluation on the full Chennai graph with \NOD{} origin--destination pairs that scores every configuration under one reference belief, splits exposure into observed and prior-only edges, compares against a hybrid baseline, checks routes against held-out official reports, and tests conformal thresholds (Sections~\ref{sec:setup}--\ref{sec:results}).
\item An account of what failed and how it was fixed (Section~\ref{sec:lessons}), and a prototype dataset of time-stamped, street-level flood evidence with negatives, assembled from fragmented public sources (Section~\ref{sec:csfe}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\subsection{Flood impacts and flood-aware routing}
Network studies quantify accessibility loss under floods~\cite{yin2016shanghai,coles2017york,green2017emergency,kasmalkar2020floods,zhou2022connectivity}, including for Indian roads~\cite{singh2018vulnerability}. Routing work usually takes the flood state from a model: stormwater inundation with flood--speed reductions~\cite{defaria2026routing}, live rainfall into a physical flood model per vehicle class~\cite{panakkal2023safer}, tunable risk weights in evacuation~\cite{jao2025float}, and Dijkstra and learning variants~\cite{li2023dijkstra,li2025drl}. Closer to our setting, gauges, social media and imagery have been fused with physics models to infer the status of individual links~\cite{panakkal2024eyes}; ambulances have been routed on satellite-derived passability~\cite{lupa2026stars}; social-media events have become a spatially decaying impedance field~\cite{fu2026social}; and an offline evacuation app treated a user's departure from the suggested path as evidence of a blocked segment~\cite{itoi2017offline}. Flood-aware routing also appears in patents~\cite{ibm2013patent,uber2020patent}. We did not find a flood router that discounts reports by age and source and lets the amount of evidence change the cost; Section~\ref{sec:results} suggests that, on our data, doing so did not help.

\subsection{Sensing road flooding}
Navigation-app reports can indicate flooded roads~\cite{praharaj2021waze,safaei2023waze} and, with traffic data, predict road inundation~\cite{yuan2023predicting}, but their coverage drifts with traffic volume~\cite{liu2023wazecoverage} and is unequal across neighbourhoods~\cite{esparza2023imbalance}, which motivates under-reporting models~\cite{agostini2024underreport}. Vehicle traces give a second signal: speed thresholds~\cite{hu2018fcd}, taxi passing rates~\cite{kong2022taxi}, probe presence~\cite{hiramoto2025probe} and a likelihood test on probe activity for closures~\cite{pietrobon2019closure}. Ultrasonic sensors measure street depth directly~\cite{mydlarz2024floodnet}. For Chennai, social-media posts have mapped 2015 inundation depths~\cite{karmegam2021chennai} and hotspots~\cite{sattaru2021utilizing}. Our replay corpus contains only positive reports; traversal data and official status statements are the most direct routes to the negative evidence it lacks (Section~\ref{sec:csfe}).

\subsection{Routing under uncertainty and ambiguity}
Stochastic and reliable shortest paths optimise expected time, variance or on-time arrival~\cite{frank1969probabilistic,fu1998expected,nie2009ontime,samaranayake2012reliable}; chance constraints~\cite{charnes1959chance} and robust optimisation~\cite{bertsimas2003robust} express caution, and safety-aware navigation trades crash or crime risk against time~\cite{galbrun2016safe,krumm2017riskaware}. When blocked roads are discovered en route, the problem becomes the Canadian Traveller Problem~\cite{papadimitriou1991ctp}. Preferring known to unknown risk is Ellsberg's ambiguity aversion~\cite{ellsberg1961risk}, formalised as maxmin expected utility~\cite{gilboa1989maxmin}; our index is a crude, per-edge version of that idea. Our first fusion followed occupancy-grid log-odds updating~\cite{elfes1989occupancy}; the current Beta form is closer to beta reputation systems, which also decay trust with age~\cite{josang2002beta}. Split conformal prediction gives distribution-free coverage under exchangeability~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal}. Landmark (ALT) search~\cite{goldberg2005alt} stays correct when no weight drops below its initial value~\cite{delling2007landmark}.

\subsection{Explaining routes and checking generated text}
Inverse optimisation explains why one path beats another~\cite{alsheeb2023explainable}, and minimal sets of congested segments explain why a traffic-aware route differs from the free-flow one~\cite{schild2025route}; drivers followed recommendations more often when they were explained~\cite{thill2018adherence}. In data-to-text generation, template-then-rewrite pipelines~\cite{kale2020t2g2} and entailment-based checking~\cite{dusek2020nli} target our problem, yet open models still make factual errors on such tasks~\cite{kasner2024quintd}. Small models run on phones~\cite{gemma2025gemma3}, but speed and energy vary widely across devices~\cite{laskaridis2024melt}.

\section{Formulation}\label{sec:model}
\subsection{Evidence}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a directed road graph with free-flow time $\tau_0(e)>0$. For edge $e$ and hazard class $c$, a prior probability $p_0(e)$ encodes susceptibility. Observation $i$ has location $x_i$, time $t_i$, polarity $y_i\in\{+1,-1\}$ and source reliability $\alpha_i\in(0,1)$. With spatial kernel $\kappa$ and class time constant $T_c$, the signed, decayed and reliability-weighted evidence on $e$ is
\begin{align}
S(e,t) &= \textstyle\sum_i y_i\,\kappa\big(d(e,x_i)\big)\,e^{-(t-t_i)/T_c}\,w(\alpha_i), \label{eq:evidence}\\
w(\alpha) &= \min\big\{1,\ \mathrm{logit}(\alpha)/\mathrm{logit}(\alpha_{\mathrm{ref}})\big\}\ \text{for}\ \alpha>0.5,\ \text{else}\ 0. \nonumber
\end{align}
A report from a source of reference reliability $\alpha_{\mathrm{ref}}$ counts as one unit; a source no better than a coin flip counts as nothing. Reports are attached to both directions of a two-way street. The prior is a susceptibility map, so it is applied only while a flood event is declared; outside an event the router uses free-flow costs.

\subsection{Belief and pessimistic index}
The belief on $e$ is a Beta distribution with the prior as pseudo-counts,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Beta}(a,b),\quad a=n_0p_0+sS^+,\quad b=n_0(1-p_0)+sS^-, \label{eq:beta}
\end{equation}
where $S^+=\max\{S,0\}$, $S^-=\max\{-S,0\}$, $n_0$ is the prior's strength and $s$ the pseudo-counts per full report. The mean is $\bar p=a/(a+b)$, and the router uses
\begin{equation}
\tilde p(e,t)=\max\big\{\bar p,\ Q_{\Phi(z)}\big(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\big)\big\}, \label{eq:pess}
\end{equation}
the $\Phi(z)$ quantile floored at the mean, with $z\ge0$ set per user class ($z=0$ commuter, $z=1.28$ pedestrian, $z=2$ emergency). We call $\tilde p$ an index rather than a bound: $n_0=2$, $s=2$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.97$ are unfitted placeholders, and the quantile carries no frequentist coverage guarantee.

\begin{proposition}[Monotone response]\label{prop:mono}
For fixed $p_0$, $n_0$, $s$ and $z$, $\tilde p$ is non-decreasing in $S$. In particular a fresh positive report never lowers $\tilde p$, opposing reports cancel, and ageing evidence moves $\tilde p$ monotonically back to the prior's own quantile.
\end{proposition}
\begin{IEEEproof}
Raising $S$ either increases $a$ (when $S\ge0$) or decreases $b$ (when $S<0$). For a Beta distribution, increasing $a$ with $b$ fixed, or decreasing $b$ with $a$ fixed, increases the distribution in the usual stochastic order, so every quantile and the mean are non-decreasing; so is their maximum~\eqref{eq:pess}. A positive report adds a non-negative term to $S$; decay multiplies every term by a factor in $(0,1]$.
\end{IEEEproof}

The prototype first used a Wald-type index, $\tilde p=\min\{1,\bar p+z\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)/(n_{\mathrm{eff}}+1)}\}$ with $\bar p$ from log-odds fusion~\cite{elfes1989occupancy} and $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_i\kappa\,e^{-(t-t_i)/T_c}$, a sum of weights that ignores reliability. Its intent was the same: thin evidence should make the router more cautious, and ageing evidence should not make a road look clear. It failed along real evidence paths.

\begin{observation}[Non-monotone Wald index]\label{obs:dip}
On an edge without observations ($n_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$), one fresh positive report from a source of reliability $\alpha$ lowers the Wald index when $\alpha<\alpha^*(p_0,z)$. For $p_0\in\{0.02,0.05,0.10\}$, numerical root finding gives $\alpha^*\in[0.624,0.635]$ at $z=1.28$ and $\alpha^*\in[0.644,0.647]$ at $z=2$.
\end{observation}
The report raises $\bar p$ from $p_0$ to $\sigma(\mathrm{logit}\,p_0+\mathrm{logit}\,\alpha)$ and halves the variance term's denominator; for $\alpha$ near 0.5 the mean barely moves while the band shrinks by $\sqrt2$. With $p_0=0.05$ and crowd reliability 0.6, the Wald index goes \ExWaldLoA, \ExWaldLoB, \ExWaldLoC, \ExWaldLoD{} for 0 to 3 reports at $z=1.28$, while~\eqref{eq:pess} goes \ExBetaLoA, \ExBetaLoB, \ExBetaLoC, \ExBetaLoD; at $z=2$ the Wald index goes \ExWaldHiA, \ExWaldHiB, \ExWaldHiC, \ExWaldHiD{} and~\eqref{eq:pess} \ExBetaHiA, \ExBetaHiB, \ExBetaHiC, \ExBetaHiD{} (both computed by the router's own code). Crowd reports make up \CrowdShare\% of our corpus, so the Wald dial penalised exactly the reports it was meant to reward.

\subsection{Edge cost}
Slowdown and harm enter separately:
\begin{equation}
w_\lambda(e,t)=\tau_0(e)\big[1+\tilde p\,(\delta-1)\big] + \lambda\,\tilde p\,s_c\,\tau_0(e), \label{eq:cost}
\end{equation}
where $\delta=\max\{1, v_0(e)/v_{\mathrm{safe}}(h)\}$ comes from the depth--disruption function of Pregnolato et~al.~\cite{pregnolato2017depth} at depth $h$ ($\delta=1$ when depth is unknown), $s_c$ is class severity and $\lambda\ge0$ the risk weight. An edge is removed when a reported depth exceeds the class threshold $h_{\max}$ and $\tilde p\ge\varepsilon$, a point surrogate for $\Pr[h>h_{\max}]\le\varepsilon$~\cite{charnes1959chance}. Both added terms are non-negative, so $w_\lambda\ge\tau_0$; landmark potentials on $\tau_0$ would therefore stay feasible~\cite{delling2007landmark}, although the prototype does not use them (Section~\ref{sec:system}).

\begin{proposition}[Bounded deterrence]\label{prop:cap}
With $\delta=1$, $w_\lambda/\tau_0=1+\lambda\tilde p s_c\le1+\lambda s_c$. A route avoiding hazardous edges of total free-flow time $T_h$ is chosen only if its extra free-flow time is below $\lambda\sum_e\tilde p_e s_c\tau_0(e)\le\lambda s_cT_h$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{IEEEproof}
Substitute $\delta=1$ in~\eqref{eq:cost}, use $\tilde p\le1$, and compare the summed costs of the two routes.
\end{IEEEproof}
With the commuter setting $\lambda=0.3$, $s_c=1$, a 60~s flooded segment justifies at most an 18~s detour even at $\tilde p=1$, and short, severe segments such as railway underpasses are cheap. No corpus record carries depth, so in all experiments $\delta=1$ and the chance constraint never fires.

\section{System as Implemented}\label{sec:system}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the design and Table~\ref{tab:status} what exists. One Dart routing package (compressed-sparse-row graph, bidirectional Dijkstra) is imported by the Flutter client and a router service, and compiled to a command-line tool for the evaluation harness, so the evaluated and shipped routers share code. A landmark (ALT) module exists and is unit-tested but is not on the query path. The belief package implements~\eqref{eq:evidence}--\eqref{eq:pess} as pure functions; property tests check Proposition~\ref{prop:mono} on a grid of prior, reliability, $z$, age and starting state, and malformed inputs are rejected at run time, since a not-a-number value would otherwise let the chance constraint fail open. The client stores observations in SQLite with an R*-tree index~\cite{beckmann1990rstar} and queues local reports in an outbox; the server keeps an append-only, grow-only observation log~\cite{shapiro2011crdt}. Records carry hybrid logical clock stamps~\cite{kulkarni2014hlc}, but synchronisation still pages by observation time, so a report made offline and uploaded late can be skipped by clients that have already synchronised past it.

Every query returns a decision record with the chosen route (duration, distance, free-flow duration, hazard penalty), rejected alternatives with their penalised edges ($\bar p$, $\tilde p$, net evidence, newest-report age), and data gaps. Tier~0 renders it with templates. Tiers~1 and~2 would ask an on-device or cloud model to rewrite it; a rewrite is shown only if it passes the checks in Table~\ref{tab:rules}, otherwise the template text is shown. The checks are symbolic and deliberately simple. On an adversarial set of \VfReject{} sentences that must be rejected and \VfAccept{} that must be accepted, the first gate accepted \VbFalseAcc{} unsafe sentences (\VbFalseAccPct\%), including ``the bridge is dry now, go ahead on Route B'' for a removed bridge; after the fixes described in Section~\ref{sec:lessons} it accepted \VfFalseAcc{} and rejected \VfFalseRej{} valid ones. The set was written by the people who fixed the gate, so this shows only that the known failures are closed; we make no claim that displayed explanations are verified.

\section{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
\subsection{Data}
\emph{Graph.} A drivable graph of Chennai from OpenStreetMap~\cite{haklay2008osm} with \NNodes{} nodes and \NEdges{} directed edges; free-flow speeds are defaults by road class.
\emph{Prior.} \NZones{} Greater Chennai Corporation flood-hazard polygons were mapped to edges within 600~m, with uncalibrated category defaults from 0.02 to 0.45. No elevation or HAND~\cite{nobre2011hand} layer was used.
\emph{Corpus.} \NObs{} observations from three OpenCity 2015 layers (\NFlood{} flood, \NWater{} waterlogging; \NOfficial{} official, \NCrowd{} crowd) were snapped to the nearest edge (median \SnapMed~m) and attached to both directions of two-way streets. The files carry no dates, so all observations share the stamp 2015-12-02T00:00Z; none has depth; all are positive. Some ``official'' points are designated vulnerable locations rather than dated observations.
\emph{Hazard entries.} \NHazEdges{} edges: \NObsEdges{} with observations and \NPriorEdges{} prior-only edges with $p_0\ge0.25$.

\subsection{Configurations and protocol}
C0 is free-flow routing. C1 removes edges with $\bar p\ge0.5$. C3 is the method of Section~\ref{sec:model} with $z=0$ at the commuter weight $\lambda=0.3$ and at $\lambda=5$ and 20. The hybrid removes edges with $\bar p>0.5$ and adds the C3 penalty with $\lambda=5$. Variants that differ only in decay (a single constant, a six-hour time-to-live, a hindsight oracle) coincide on a single-timestamp corpus and appear only in the calibration study. Parameters were fixed before the run.

All routes come from the production router (a batch mode of the command-line tool) for \NOD{} origin--destination pairs drawn with a pinned seed; none was disconnected under any configuration. An earlier version of our harness scored each configuration under its own belief and counted penalty seconds as travel time, which made configurations incomparable. Here every route is scored under one reference belief, the posterior mean $\bar p$ of the C3 model at the replay clock, and detours are in free-flow time. Metrics are $\sum_{e\in P}\bar p_e$ (expected hazardous edges per route), split into observed and prior-only edges; the share of routes containing an edge with $\bar p\ge0.5$; and extra free-flow time relative to C0. Paired differences carry 95\% bootstrap intervals over pairs (\BootB{} resamples). Because the reference belief is the model's own, we add one check that does not use it: official reports are held out of both routing beliefs, which are built from the prior alone or from prior plus crowd reports, and we count edges with an official report on each route.

\subsection{Calibration study}
With no confirmed-absent reports, the label is a source holdout: a crowd-reported edge is positive if it also has an official report. Predictors see the prior and crowd reports, with report ages of 0, 1, 6, 24, 72 and 168~h simulated from the single timestamp. The pool has \CrowdEdges{} crowd edges at six ages (\CrowdRows{} rows, \PosEdges{} positive edges) plus \NoRepEdges{} randomly sampled edges without reports, labelled negative, for \CalN{} rows and \CalPos{} positives. Baselines are the prior alone, a single decay constant (C2), a six-hour time-to-live (C4), a beta reputation model with forgetting~\cite{josang2002beta} and climatology. We report the Brier score with its decomposition~\cite{brier1950verification,murphy1973partition}, the Brier skill score against climatology and against the prior, and AUROC~\cite{fawcett2006roc}.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}
\subsection{RQ1: the default barely acts; larger weights trade time for exposure}
The default commuter setting ($z=0$, $\lambda=0.3$) changed \ChgThree{} of \NOD{} routes at a \DetThree\% mean detour and changed expected hazardous edges per route by \DThreeZero{} (95\% CI [\DThreeZerolo, \DThreeZerohi]), almost all of it on edges with observations (\DObsThreeZero) rather than prior-only edges (\DPriorThreeZero{} [\DPriorThreeZerolo, \DPriorThreeZerohi]). \HrThree\% of its routes still crossed an edge with $\bar p\ge0.5$, against \HrZero\% for C0 (Table~\ref{tab:sweep}). Proposition~\ref{prop:cap} explains the small effect: at $\lambda=0.3$ a hazardous edge costs at most 1.3 times its free-flow time. Hard blocking (C1) changed \ChgOne{} routes at a \DetOne\% detour and removed every $\bar p\ge0.5$ crossing by construction, but left total exposure unchanged (\DOneZero{} [\DOneZerolo, \DOneZerohi]): it moved exposure onto prior-only edges (\DPriorOneZero{} [\DPriorOneZerolo, \DPriorOneZerohi]). Larger weights lowered exposure steadily (Fig.~\ref{fig:pareto}): $\lambda=5$ by \DFiveZero{} at a \DetThreeFive\% detour and $\lambda=20$ by \DTwentyZero{} at \DetThreeTwenty\%.

\subsection{RQ2: the soft cost helps, the crowd evidence does not}
Fig.~\ref{fig:decomp} splits exposure by edge type. The hybrid lowered expected hazardous edges by \DHybZero{} [\DHybZerolo, \DHybZerohi] relative to C0. C3 at $\lambda=5$ did slightly worse than the hybrid: \DFiveHyb{} [\DFiveHyblo, \DFiveHybhi] more exposure per route, all of it on edges with observations (\DObsFiveHyb{} [\DObsFiveHyblo, \DObsFiveHybhi]) and none on prior-only edges (\DPriorFiveHyb{} [\DPriorFiveHyblo, \DPriorFiveHybhi]), at a \DetThreeFive\% against \DetHyb\% detour. The gain over hard blocking therefore comes from adding a soft cost at all, not from the way C3 weighs evidence.

Against held-out official reports (Table~\ref{tab:holdout}), routes built on prior plus crowd reports crossed \emph{more} officially reported edges than routes built on the prior alone, at both risk weights, and the paired intervals exclude zero. On this check, crowd evidence did not merely fail to help; it moved routes toward reported places. The official layers share the label problems noted below, so this is weak evidence, but it is the only check in this paper that does not reuse the model's own belief.

\subsection{RQ2 continued: calibration and coverage}
Table~\ref{tab:cal} gives the calibration results. Every model scored worse than climatology (Brier \CliBrier), and the prior alone scored best: C3's skill against the prior was \BssPriorThree, and on the crowd pool at report age zero the prior scored \BrierPriorAgeZero{} and C3 \BrierThreeAgeZero. Adding crowd evidence worsened the belief, and the score improved as crowd weight decayed. Resolution was near zero ($\ResThree$). The pooled AUROC is inflated by the report-free negatives; on the crowd pool it was \AucThreeCrowd{} for C3 against \AucPriorCrowd{} for the prior. Class-specific decay (C3) was indistinguishable from a single constant (C2), but with simulated ages this is not a test of decay. The beta baseline has no base rate and predicts at least 0.5 on every reported edge, which explains its score.

The reliability diagrams (Fig.~\ref{fig:rel}) show predictions far above observed frequencies. The label explains part of this: a positive requires an official and a crowd report on the same edge, so only \PosEdges{} of the \NOfficialEdges{} edges with an official report enter the pool as positives. The label is closer to a test of co-location at edge resolution than of flooding.

Finally, we asked whether calibration could at least give the index a stated meaning. Following pre-registered rules, label-conditional split conformal thresholds~\cite{angelopoulos2023conformal} at $\alpha=0.1$ kept their coverage of officially reported edges on a spatially blocked split (\CfCov), but flagged \CfFf\% of edges without a report (\CfFfPrior\% for the prior alone), while the fixed rule $\bar p\ge0.5$ covered \CfCOneCov{} of them. A route-level version, ``every reported edge on the route is flagged in 9 of 10 routes'', met its coverage only by setting the threshold at the prior's floor (\CbTau), which flags \CbShare\% of route time. Calibration works as mathematics here; the scores it is given cannot support a useful statement.

\subsection{RQ3}
Under the Wald index, Observation~\ref{obs:dip} held on the corpus parameters: crowd reliability 0.6 sits just below $\alpha^*$, so for $z>0$ the first one or two crowd reports on an edge lowered $\tilde p$, and at $z=2$ the index saturated at 1 on every prior-only edge with $p_0\ge0.25$. The Beta index of~\eqref{eq:pess} removes both effects (Proposition~\ref{prop:mono} and the worked example in Section~\ref{sec:model}). The replay cannot show that the new index helps: with one timestamp and no independent labels, it only shows that the old failure is gone.

\section{What Failed, and What We Changed}\label{sec:lessons}
\emph{One-directional evidence.} Each observation was first snapped to a single directed edge, so a flooded two-way street was penalised in one direction only. Evidence is now attached to both directions; every result above uses the corrected corpus.

\emph{Caution in the wrong place.} The Wald index penalised the first weak reports and saturated on prior-only edges; it was replaced by~\eqref{eq:pess}. The prior was applied whether or not an event was under way; an event state now gates it, set from satellite rain with an operator override, which reacts hours late and uses placeholder thresholds.

\emph{Explanations.} The gate passed unsafe sentences, the template said a route ``avoids'' a corridor it partly crossed and reported a delay that compared penalised cost with plain travel time, and when the template failed its own check the client showed an error instead of a route. On the developers' case set the checks now catch reversed comparisons and false route-level avoidance, delays are computed in free-flow time, and a failed template falls back to a minimal safe text with the route still shown.

\emph{Offline claim.} The design is offline-first, and the client has been installed and run on one Android phone, but no latency, memory, battery or offline measurement has been made (Table~\ref{tab:status}).

\section{Toward Independent Labels: A Prototype Evidence Dataset}\label{sec:csfe}
Every result above is limited by the corpus: one timestamp, no depth and no negatives. As a first step we assembled fragments that
already exist into one table, Chennai Street Flood Evidence (CSFE, prototype), and documented it with a datasheet~\cite{gebru2021datasheets}. It holds \CsfeObs{} statements about places (\CsfeCrowd{} crowd, \CsfeOfficial{} official, \CsfeNews{} news): the 2015 corpus, official hotspot layers with depth classes, time-stamped photo reports from the state's flood-monitoring app, and facts hand-extracted from news reports of \CsfeNewsEvents{} rain events (2021--2026), each with its link, publication time and a short quote. \CsfeNeg{} rows are negatives (a subway not waterlogged, open, or waterlogged but open), and \CsfeTimed{} carry a time to the day or better. Each statement is snapped to the graph in both directions and joined to the same day's rain from \CsfeGauges{} city gauges (\CsfeGaugeDays{} gauge-days), and a status timeline follows \CsfeSubways{} railway subways across events.

Building it taught two things. First, the gauges' day convention had to be inferred from the rain series itself (storm totals sit on the readings dated the days of heavy rain); our first assumption was off by a day, which invalidated a pre-registered test, and a build fix followed, so the run below is exploratory. Second, the data cannot yet answer the simplest passability question. Predicting whether a subway report says ``closed'' from rain, leaving one event out, used \BoneRows{} rows from only \BoneEvents{} events, because the gauge record has gaps in 2020--2022 and after February 2026, where most subway negatives fall; two of the three events were all-closed lists. Rain gave no evidence of skill over the base rate (Brier skill \BoneRainBss, 95\% interval over events [\BoneRainBsslo, \BoneRainBsshi]). The lesson is concrete: collect explicit open and not-waterlogged statements during events the gauges cover, with the time each status applied rather than when it was published.

\section{Threats to Validity}\label{sec:threats}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Circular reference.} Exposure is measured under the model's own belief; only the held-out official check is external, and its labels are partly susceptibility designations.
\item \emph{Corpus.} One event, one timestamp, no depth, no negative reports, so decay, the chance constraint and false avoidance are untested.
\item \emph{Independence.} Correlated crowd reports of one flood inflate certainty in~\eqref{eq:evidence}.
\item \emph{Defaults.} Prior probabilities, speeds, $n_0$, $s$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $T_c$ are not fitted; one city.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
We asked whether a router that fuses a flood prior with decaying crowd reports, and becomes more cautious when evidence is thin, routes better on a real city graph. On the 2015 Chennai corpus the answer is no. The default penalty was too weak to change many routes, as Proposition~\ref{prop:cap} predicts. Where larger penalties helped, a simple block-plus-penalty baseline did as well or better. Against held-out official reports, crowd evidence moved routes toward reported edges, and it worsened calibration relative to the prior. Our first pessimistic index lowered caution after weak reports; its Beta replacement cannot, but the replay cannot show that it helps. These are results about one historical event with poor labels, not a verdict on crowd evidence in general. The next step is data rather than modelling: a time-stamped corpus with independent passability labels, from probe-vehicle traces~\cite{hiramoto2025probe,pietrobon2019closure}, depth sensors~\cite{mydlarz2024floodnet} or the official status statements our prototype dataset gathers, collected during events that rain gauges cover; and a measured pass rate for model-written explanations on a low-cost phone.
